title: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky

teacherSummary.text: Marshal Jack Potter rides a Pullman car home to Yellow Sky with his new bride, anxious because he married without telling the town. Meanwhile drunken Scratchy Wilson terrorizes the empty street with revolvers, looking for his old enemy Potter. Scratchy confronts the unarmed marshal, hears he is married, says 'I s'pose it's all off now,' and walks away.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “A newly married pair had boarded this coach at San Antonio” slowly and put it in my own words: A newly married couple has boarded the Pullman train at San Antonio, heading west. Next, craft. I notice the plain, almost reporter-like sentence, which treats a wedding trip as an ordinary news item. The strongest word is “married”: the marriage is the quiet event that will end the town's gunfight days, so the plain word carries the plot. Then, effect. What does Crane want us to notice about this couple from the start? My answer: Crane opens with something tame and modern, a couple on a fancy train, to show that the tame, settled world from back east is arriving in the West; the old gunfighter will be beaten not by a bullet but by a wife.
